Lower doses of heparin may be effec- tive and safer, particularly if glycoprotein IIb/IIIa-recep- tor antagonists are also used, and a target ACT of 200 to 250 seconds has been suggested;2,3 however, an analysis9 found no clear relation between heparin dose and outcome. • Low-molecular-weight heparins have been used, al- though evidence for their efficacy is limited;2,3,10,11 a meta-analysis12 that included mostly non-blinded stud- ies found that low-molecular-weight heparin was as safe and effective as unfractionated heparin, and further studies13,14 have come to similar conclusions. • Direct thrombin inhibitors may be another alterna- tive;2,3,11 bivalirudin appears to be as effective as heparin,15,16 while a study with desirudin17 found fewer early ischaemic events but no long term benefit com- pared with heparin. • Fondaparinux has also been tried,18 but the risk of cath- eter thrombosis may be increased and additional unfrac- tionated heparin is recommended at the time of the pro- cedure.3,11 Antiplatelet drugs have an important role in reducing acute thrombotic complications and in long-term treat- ment. • In patients undergoing surgical bypass, they are not usu- ally started until after the procedure since they increase the risk of bleeding, and patients who are already taking such drugs usually have them withheld for several days before elective surgery.19 Continuation of antiplatelet therapy pre-operatively increases blood loss and the need for blood products,20-22 although there is some ev- idence that use of aspirin pre-operatively may improve outcomes.23 • In patients undergoing PCI, the use of antiplatelet drugs with anticoagulants during the procedure is of estab- lished benefit. Aspirin is considered standard thera- py,2,3,11 and patients who are not already taking aspirin are usually given a loading dose at least 2 hours before the procedure; a thienopyridine such as clopidogrel or ticlopidine may be used in patients unable to tolerate aspirin. However, aspirin does not completely inhibit platelet function and combination therapy and more po- tent drugs have also been studied. • Use of clopidogrel with aspirin improves outcomes and is now generally recommended,2,3,11 although the dose and timing have been debated. Pretreatment with clopi- dogrel appears to be most effective, but the increased bleeding risk may be of concern if emergency surgery is required.
